Current artefact_v1 and the original thesis v1/ (still present on the v3 branch, absent from this branch's working tree) are NOT two different graphs: both query the same Neo4j herb-eval database, with v3/pipelines/artefact_v1.py defaulting to NEO4J_DATABASE=herb-eval and HERB_TAG_RUN_ID=pilot_full_herb and saying so in its own module docstring. What changed is the retrieval engine and the embeddings sitting on top of that graph, not the graph itself. Old v1/ was the browser workbench - retrieval.ts at about 818 lines plus interpreter.ts - with two-pass interpret producing LLM facet scores per tag, per-facet kNN grounding at minSim about 0.78, one Cypher score product, an optional hard-gate filter, e5-small embeddings and chunk text stored directly in the graph. Current artefact_v1 does one-pass interpret emitting {description, parts, gate} with no numbers from the model, per-part multi-k pooling at 8/16/32/64 into an average-linkage dendrogram, a shared walk of anchors widening tightest-first, plus description-area clustering, with stated scope corroborating rather than hard-gating, nemotron embeddings, and chunk content stripped from the live graph and resolved from raw source by locator and hash. v3/artefact/ is a separate, still-unfinished third thing

Why the old eval was reported cheap and the current one expensive is mostly a fixed-evidence-budget effect rather than a retrieval-efficiency difference. The old thesis eval retrieved a median of 15 chunks against Lucene's 40 AND applied a matched cap to both arms (answer_max_chunks=40, 1800 chars per chunk, the same rule for graph and Lucene), so the graph's answer_in came out around 9.4k tokens against the baseline's ~24k largely because its median sat under that shared cap while Lucene's filled it. Current artefact_v1 lost both advantages: it always fills k=50 from pools of hundreds to thousands of candidates, and ships full resolved raw chunk text with no truncation cap at all, with a reported median around 240k chars against vector's ~13k. It also pays extra per-query costs the baselines do not - haiku interpret, NIM query embeds, and the Neo4j walk itself. The matched truncation cap was dropped when the harness was rewritten, not disproven, so reintroducing it is a legitimate cost lever, but only applied identically across all three arms and only with the caveat that capped-quality numbers are a different measurement; and any reintroduced cap has to work at the chunk or char level, because truncate_k slicing context_ids[:k] is invalid for the artefact arm. The specific cost multipliers are relayed from a separate analysis session and were not independently re-derived from raw run logs
